author: avatarsd
body:
Executes the first half of the #1505 ruling: the sizing guide's caveat 2 is corrected **before** the production candidate lands, so the guide is truthful whether it is read now or between the two merges.

### What was wrong

Caveat 2 of `docs/reference/22-backpressure-and-sizing.md` said the HANDLER fan-out pays a clone the storing path avoids, and told the reader: *do not choose HANDLER for throughput on a heavily-subscribed vertex.*

Both halves mislead sizing:

- **Wrong axis.** The clone is a per-**write** term, not a per-delivery one. It is **flat in fan-out** — a fan-out-**zero** handler vertex pays it in full, before discovering there is nobody to notify. Subscriber count is not the variable.
- **Wrong direction below the knee.** While the rope fits its inline link capacity the clone touches no allocator, and HANDLER is the **cheaper** role, because it skips the LKV publish the retaining roles pay for.

### The numbers it now carries

From #1505's report on the instruments landed in #1516 (`bench_source_role`, `bench_source_role_alloc`; x86-64 `-O3`, best of 5 interleaved rounds, p50 ns per write):

| links | fan | STORED_VALUE | HANDLER |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0 | 80 | **70** |
| 1 | 4 | 120 | **110** |
| 4 | 0 | **130** | 170 |
| 4 | 4 | **170** | 210 |

Allocations per write at 1 link: **1 (HANDLER) vs 2 (STORED_VALUE)**. The inline knee is **measured between 2 and 3 links**, not read off a private constant.

### Written to survive the gap

The candidate that removes the clone is ruled and lands next. The caveat states the current-truth sizing rule, then says in one paragraph what changes when the candidate lands and what survives it (the "HANDLER is cheaper" half). Read between the two merges it is accurate; read after, the closing tense-fix is folded into the candidate PR rather than costing a third one.

### Verification

- `tools/check_doc_citations.py`: **OK 483 doc citations verified**. The paragraph's `core/src/graph.cpp:2202` pin still resolves — the `:stats` field arm (#1519) moved `graph.cpp` but not above that line — so no repin was needed.
- Docs-only diff; no source, no spec, no wire surface.

### Perf gate

**No exposure** — documentation only, `perf.yml` is path-filtered and this touches no benched path.

Refs #1505.

author: gavin-borges
body:
Closes the repository's only open code-scanning alert and lands the security
work that was sitting uncommitted in the working tree, each item re-verified
against the live platform rather than carried forward from notes.

## The security notification

CodeQL alert #79 (`py/log-injection`, CWE-117) on `api/main.py` was the only
open alert of any kind: Dependabot is 106 alerts, all fixed, 0 open, and secret
scanning is 0 open.

`api/main.py` is the project's only HTTP entrypoint, and both of its exception
handlers interpolated request-derived values into a log record whose format is
one line per record, so a CR or LF in a field could append a fabricated second
line to an audit trail.

**Reported honestly: this was not exploitable.** Both fields carry anchored
Pydantic patterns and pydantic 2.13.4 compiles them with the Rust regex engine,
which rejected every CR/LF payload tested. But that protection is incidental and
engine-dependent - the identical anchored pattern under Python's own `re.match`
accepts a trailing newline where `re.fullmatch` does not - so widening
`_ALLELE_PATTERN` to admit HLA-C or three-field alleles would have made it live.

`exc` is sanitized alongside the two named fields because
`PeptideNotInPanelError(sequence)` raises using the caller's own peptide, so an
exception message can echo request-derived text back verbatim. Sanitizing only
the obvious fields would have cleared the alert while leaving the channel open.

## What else is here

| Commit | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `fdd7fba` | CWE-117 fix + 7 tests, incl. an AST guard over every logging call in the module |
| `532a1d0` | `persist-credentials: false` on 19 checkout steps; retired `apply_protection.sh`; corrected the CI gate map |
| `9e336d5` | `torch.load(weights_only=True)` enforced by AST scan (SEC-13) |
| `c80e175` | ENC-1 Windows-console crash + a 6-test CI gate for the encoding rule |
| `f5fc5e8` | CHANGELOG; narrowed an overstated third-party comparison claim |
| `d9506cb` | SEC-14: setuptools build-system floor raised above the CVE line |
| `4febc26` | Two unbindable claims caught by the pre-push audit |
| `cafa83a` | A false build-isolation claim retracted from the SEC-14 entry |

Two of these are worth calling out because they make SESTRAV look **weaker**,
which is the direction that matters:

- **`tools/apply_protection.sh` is now inert.** Running it would have *blocked
  every future merge*, not weakened protection: it looked up the ruleset by the
  wrong name, so the lookup missed, fell through to `POST`, and would have
  created a *second* ruleset requiring the context `SESTRAV CI / test (3.13)`,
  which nothing reports. Rulesets are additive, so every PR would have been
  pending forever. It keeps the live ruleset as an inert reference block,
  machine-diffed at 6/6 writable top-level keys and 34/34 leaf fields.
- **`SECURITY.md`'s gate map was wrong.** Bandit and Dependency Review were
  labeled "Blocking"; neither is a required status check, so neither can gate a
  merge. Dependency Review's severity is `moderate`, not `high`. CodeQL is the
  only tool that blocks, via the ruleset's code-scanning rule.

## Verification

Full fast-test gate green (the pre-push hook ran it), ruff clean, mypy clean
(0 issues / 63 files), scoped Bandit 0 medium/high, all 16 new tests pass. ENC-1
reproduced as a real outage and confirmed fixed: `check_repo_status.py` exited 1
under `PYTHONIOENCODING=cp1252` and now exits 0, and
`precompute_self_similarity.py --help` did the same under `ascii`.

Every count was re-derived rather than trusted: 21 checkout steps across 14
files, 19 changed across 12, 20 now explicit, with `dco.yml` the one deliberate
exception because its required `check_dco` job runs `git fetch origin` after
checkout.

**Three false claims were produced by this change set's own correction passes
and are all retracted in it** (`4febc26`, `cafa83a`), with reproducible evidence
behind each replacement. The last one was caught only by adversarial review: the
SEC-14 entry claimed a `>=84.0.0` floor would break local builds on a box
carrying setuptools 83.0.0. PEP 517 builds are isolated, so that is false in
both directions - measured, a probe package pinned `>=84.0.0` builds fine under
ambient 83.0.0, and the shipped `>=83.0.0` floor provisions 84.0.0 into the
isolated env anyway. The cited verification had called the backend in-process,
bypassing the very isolation it claimed to test.

Semgrep could not be run locally (blocked by an OS Application Control policy on
the dev machine); CI is authoritative for it.

author: tiagocameli
body:
> "pensava que iamos tirar as aplicacoes do aplicativo como voce disse"

Ele está certo e eu tinha parado no meio. As migrations anteriores tiraram a varredura de onde ela **mentia** (resultado, saldo, fluxo de caixa, aging, KPIs), mas os 257 lançamentos continuaram na base, e portanto continuaram ocupando linha em Lançamentos, Pagamentos, Recebimentos e no extrato do cliente. Eu tinha até escrito no plano que a movimentação "continua visível num bloco próprio", que é exatamente o que ele não queria.

Um lançamento que não é resultado, não é caixa, não é saldo e não é dívida não é documento financeiro da empresa: é linha de extrato que a carga trouxe.

## Arquivo morto, não exclusão simples

`fn_excluir_lancamento` não servia: ela recusa lançamento com parcela paga (os 257 estão todos pagos) e faz `DELETE` de verdade, porque `lancamentos` não tem soft delete.

Então segui o padrão que o projeto já usa em `arquivo_morto` (há tabelas `*_20260807` de uma limpeza anterior): **cópia integral antes de apagar**, com o dia no nome. São 257 lançamentos, 257 parcelas e 257 rateios, todas as colunas. Para desfazer, basta reinserir das três tabelas.

Conferido antes de apagar: os 257 são todos origem `manual`, nenhum tem anexo, nenhum está em `recebimentos`, `extrato_transacoes` está vazia, e parcelas, rateios, formas e eventos de parcela caem por CASCADE.

## Provas

Em transação desfeita, antes de aplicar:

| o que não podia mudar | resultado |
|---|---|
| Saldo das cinco contas | **idêntico** |
| Fluxo de caixa | **idêntico** (R$ 92.247.411,92) |
| DRE operacional e financeiro | **idênticos** ao centavo |
| Custo por centro de custo | 27 dos 28 centros idênticos |

A primeira prova acusou "custo por centro mudou: **f**" e eu **não aceitei**: refiz medindo centro por centro, porque "mudou" podia ser uma obra perdendo custo. Não era. Mudou só o próprio centro **"Investimentos"**, que sai de R$ 10.854.817,87 para inexistente.

Ele era o **terceiro maior "centro de custo" de 2026**, acima de obras reais como o Ramal do Gama, e estava cadastrado com tipo `obra` — então aparecia entre as obras no filtro e na escala do gráfico. Era o gap que eu tinha relatado dois PRs atrás.

A migration carrega essa checagem embutida: se qualquer obra mudar de valor, ela aborta em vez de aplicar.

## Duas limpezas de acabamento

- O centro **"Investimentos" foi desativado**, não excluído: é cadastro, o arquivo morto aponta para ele, e desativar volta num clique.
- A coluna **"Em aplicação"** da aba Contas bancárias passa a nascer **oculta**. Sem lançamento de movimentação ela mostraria "-" nas cinco contas, e coluna que só mostra traço é ruído. Continua existindo porque volta a servir no dia em que entrar uma aplicação de verdade, e posição aplicada negativa é impossível e precisa aparecer.

## O que se perde, e vale dizer

`fn_rel_posicao_aplicacao` acusava **−R$ 3.571.015,96** na Caixa, um impossível que servia de sinal de "falta importar extrato". Sem os lançamentos, ela zera.

**O problema não desaparece:** o saldo da Caixa continua em −R$ 3.571.015,96 e continua precisando de rebase com o saldo aplicado real. Perde-se o diagnóstico automático da causa, não o sintoma.

A função, a natureza `movimentacao` e as duas categorias **ficam**: são o mecanismo que impede o problema de voltar. Aplicação lançada de agora em diante nasce fora do resultado, do saldo e do caixa por construção, sem precisar desta limpeza de novo.

## Estado final

| | Antes | Agora |
|---|---:|---:|
| Lançamentos | 6.472 | **6.215** |
| De varredura | 257 | **0** |
| No arquivo morto | 0 | **257** |

DRE de 2026 agora tem só operacional (R$ 26.906.804,77 de receita e R$ 39.809.311,91 de despesa) e financeira (R$ 10.382,86). A linha de movimentação deixou de existir.

author: paralin
body:
A matched solicit stream proves routing agreement between two peers, never content trust. `exchangeSnapshots` adopted a peer's full `SOState` wholesale whenever its root seqno was higher, so any peer that matched the solicitation could replace local shared-object state with an unverified config, grants, and ops.

This change validates inbound snapshot elements before the higher-seqno adoption rule: the resulting config must keep the local session peer as a readable participant, and every root grant and queued op carried in the snapshot must hold a signature that validates against that config's participants. A failing snapshot closes the stream. Remote ops now verify the signer against the current local participants at the sync layer before queueing; `SOState.QueueOperation` already re-validates under the state lock, so this surfaces rejection at warn level instead of a debug-level swallow.

Scope note: this is defense in depth against misdirected or corrupted state. It does **not** verify config authorship or lineage. The sending peer may have self-authored the received config; nothing here verifies who wrote it. Full config-head verification requires `VerifyConfigChain` over the sender's `SOConfigChange` entries, which neither `SOSyncMessage` nor any p2p-side store carries today; closing that chain-lineage gap is a separate prerequisite.

Tests: two snapshot rejections fail against the ungated code and pass after (excluded local peer, tampered root grant); one convergence test pins that legitimate higher-seqno adoption still works; two op tests pin the existing host-level signature enforcement through the sync path.

author: yanib-app[bot]
body:
Yanib generated this file. **Nothing changes until this is merged.**

## What `.yanib.yml` does

It declares this repository's **surfaces**, the places where an *addition* may represent a capability change worth reviewing: a new API route an integrator can call, a new model a downstream query can carry, or a new environment variable the next deploy may need.

On each push to the default branch, Yanib checks the diff against these paths. Matching added files and added diff lines become evidence-backed review candidates. When notifications are enabled, delivery follows the configured routes; related docs can also be marked for review. These structural rules narrow the queue but do not prove downstream impact on their own.

## Why these surfaces

The tree given for this repo stops at 'src/agentbarrier/' with no children listed, so the surfaces below are inferred from the explicit repo brief ('adapters for frameworks, MCP gateway, approval API, and dashboard implementation', 'CLI commands for operational controls') and corroborated by the matching test files (test_*_adapter.py per framework, test_mcp_gateway.py, test_approval_api.py, test_dashboard.py, test_cli.py). I included framework-adapters as new_file because the brief explicitly calls out an 'adapter pattern' where one new file equals one new supported framework, a clear external capability for integrators. I used pattern detection for approval-api-routes, mcp-gateway-routes, and dashboard-routes because these are FastAPI/Starlette-backed HTTP surfaces (per the stated stack) where new capability arrives as an added route decorator inside an existing router file, not as a new file per endpoint; refactoring a handler's body stays silent. cli-commands captures newly added operator-facing subcommands (pause/resume/limits) since that's explicitly named as a convention and each new command is a new lever for operators, distinct from internal CLI plumbing changes. I deliberately left out a prisma_schema surface since the stack uses SQLite directly with no schema.prisma in the tree, omitted docs/env-var surfaces since no .env.example or comparable config file is visible, and excluded tests, examples, tools, and docs directories themselves since growth there (fixtures, reference scripts, audit tooling, prose) doesn't create a capability for someone outside the owning team reading diffs.

## Merging this is what activates it

Until then Yanib runs its defaults for this repo: new `app/api/**/route.ts` files, and the Prisma schema. Once merged, the file is the source of truth and takes effect on the next push.

## It's meant to be edited

Change the globs to match your layout, point `docs:` at the files that actually go stale when each surface grows, add a `notify:` list to route a surface to specific channels, and delete any surface that would fire on noise, one noisy surface is how the whole feature gets muted. Yanib reads the file again on any push that edits it.

[Format reference and full documentation](https://github.com/binaydhakal/Yanib/blob/main/docs/surface-detection.md)

author: chrischall
body:
Follow-up to #133, which squash-merged at 21:32:51 — about forty seconds before the first of these fixes was pushed, so none of its review feedback reached `main`. Same race as #132 → #133. Rebased onto the merge here.

All four findings from the #133 auto-review, all valid.

## 1. A regression test that could not fail

The review pointed out that the test guarding `extractPdfText`'s defensive copy was vacuous: `base64` and the file write both complete *before* extraction runs, so `readFileSync(path).length` matched with or without the copy. Verified by deleting `Uint8Array.from` and re-running — the test stayed green.

`bytes` is the field read *after* extraction, and a detached buffer reports 0 there. With that assertion added, the same deletion goes red:

```
× extracts the text layer of a PDF receipt
AssertionError: expected +0 to be 579
```

And the copy really is load-bearing — confirmed directly against unpdf rather than assumed:

```
before: 579 bytes
extracted ok: "MPHSBANDS Band Shirts\nTotal 129.00 USD"
AFTER (no copy): 0 bytes
```

## 2. `extract_text` gated on a header servers get wrong

The review suggested gating on `isPdf(asset.bytes)`. Correct — but the narrow version leaves the same wrong type naming the file, which I checked before choosing:

```
application/pdf            -> application/pdf            (file: .pdf)
application/force-download -> application/force-download  (file: .bin)   ← refused text AND misnamed
application/x-pdf          -> application/x-pdf           (file: .bin)   ← same
application/octet-stream   -> application/pdf             (file: .pdf)
```

So the fix goes one level up: in `resolveMimeType`, **magic bytes now win over the declared Content-Type**. Anything sniffing can't place still falls back to the declared type, so `image/heic` keeps its type and `.heic` extension — there's a test. One value feeds the extension, the inline block's type and the text gate, so they can't disagree.

## 3. The fail-loudly error discarded the reason that mattered

`reason` only described the *write*, so a read-only server plus `extract_text: true` on a photographed receipt answered with *"Re-run with … extract_text:true"* — advice to repeat the call that just failed, with `This PDF has no text layer…` thrown away.

The error now leads with whatever actually blocked the content and falls back to the generic advice only when neither applies. Every text note also ends with a way forward, so it's a complete answer in the success path too.

## 4. `inline_skipped` advised a write that had already run

It said "fetch it with `write:true`" in both states where that can't help — when the write succeeded (`path` is in the same result) and when it failed (`write_error` is too). The tail now keys off `path`.

## Testing

`npm test` → **94 passing** (up from 91). New: mis-declared `application/force-download` PDF → `application/pdf`, `.pdf`, and extracted text; unsniffable `image/heic` keeps its declared type; read-only + scanned PDF names the missing text layer and points at `inline:true` while asserting it does *not* say `extract_text:true`; `inline_skipped` points at the path and not at `write:true` when the write succeeded; plus the `bytes` assertion above.

`tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build` clean.

Live verification against `4644814211` still pending a release — I'll retry once this ships.

author: mikalstill
body:
Nine of the ten open consistency-audit issues on this repository, one
commit each, oldest first. Stacked on a single branch to keep the CI
load to one run rather than nine.

| Issue | Audit | What changed |
|-------|-------|--------------|
| #185 | Secret scanning in CI | A `credential_scan` job running a pinned gitleaks 8.16.0 through `tools/gitleaks-scan.sh`, plus `.gitleaks.toml` |
| #295 | Pre-push audit file | `llm-doc-discipline` and `plan-phase-references` pasted verbatim into `PUSH-AUDIT.md` |
| #296 | sfui vendored copy | Re-vendored at canonical `190383a` |
| #310 | Renovate | The pre-commit manager enabled, plus a `customManagers` regex and a `shellcheck` group |
| #334 | Links out of `docs/` are absolute | The one escaping relative link made absolute |
| #341 | Plan index | Two status cells cut back to `In progress` |
| #342 | Plan template | `plan-status-vocabulary` added |
| #346 | LLM context linting | Both Claude skills moved to `<name>/SKILL.md` |
| #347 | LLM context linting in pre-commit and CI | skillsaw in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` and in `sanity_checks` |
| #348 | CI review automation | `pr-re-review.yml` replaced with the fleet template |

## Two of these are not paperwork

**#348 closed a live fork pull request hole.** `pr-re-review.yml`
hand-rolled its trigger handling instead of using
`shakenfist/actions/pr-bot-trigger@main`, and so never inherited the
action's fork guard. The job checked out the pull request's code onto a
claude-code runner holding a write-scoped token, gated only on the
commenter's write access to *this* repository -- and a maintainer typing
the trigger phrase on a fork's pull request is enough. The template also
brings a merge-ref checkout (the old file reviewed against the default
branch, so it judged changes by the conventions as they were *before*
them) and `persist-credentials: false`.

**#346 means neither Claude skill has ever loaded.** A skill is
`<skills dir>/<name>/SKILL.md`; a bare markdown file in `.claude/skills/`
is inert, and is not linted either, because nothing discovers it as a
skill. `AGENTS.md` has been telling agents that a skill "walks the full
workflow" for adding a source type. skillsaw now reports `Skills: 2`
where it previously found none.

## Worth a reviewer's attention

- **The credential scan is deliberately not gated on `check_paths`.** It
  is the only job in either tier that runs on a documentation-only
  change, because a credential pasted into a code sample is a
  credential. It also scans the review notes under `.vscode/`, which is
  why `.pre-commit-config.yaml` scopes its rewriting hooks rather than
  excluding those files outright -- that comment pointed at #185 as
  future work and now points at the scanner.
- **Re-vendoring sfui changes served assets.** `sf-data-table.js` is new
  (nothing loads it yet), and `sf-theme.js` now sets `Secure` on the
  theme cookie. That flag is conditional on `https:`, so the http-only
  demo stack and direct-qemu lane still persist the preference.
- **Enabling Renovate's pre-commit manager needed more than one line.**
  shellcheck is pinned twice -- as a hook revision and as a
  `shellcheck-py` dependency of the shellcheck tox environment -- and
  both files say to keep them in lockstep. Renovate has no tox manager,
  so it would have bumped the hook alone and left CI and the hook
  disagreeing about what passes, with the comments still insisting they
  agreed.
- **`automated_reviewer` now needs `credential_scan`.** Its `needs:` list
  is the "review only once CI has passed" gate, and the new scan is a
  smoke-tier job it was not waiting for.

## Not in this branch

**#227 (human review coverage)** is untouched. It is restored by doing
review sessions over the 62 files needing review, and the signature on
the stamping commit *is* the attestation -- so it is not work an agent
can do. The new files here add to that backlog.

**#357** is filed for the gap #185 could not close: the SPICE console
token is 48 characters of unadorned base62, so no rule can tell a leaked
one from any other identifier. Giving it an `sfk_`-style prefix is a
wire-format change to a value SPICE carries as a password.

Existing plan phase tables are also left alone. `PLAN-proxy-dev-releases.md`
still has `Complete (merged in PR #314, 2026-08-16)` in its own table,
which the vocabulary added in #342 does not allow, but no audit checks
that column and dropping where the work landed would lose more than it
gains.

## Verification

Run locally on every commit: `pre-commit run --all-files` (actionlint,
shellcheck, skillsaw, flake8, unit tests) and
`tools/check-required-checks.sh`. The gitleaks scan is clean over 755
commits, its positive control fires, and a temporary commit containing a
real RSA key correctly failed it before being reverted. The vendored sfui
copy diffs clean against canonical both before and after the sync, and
all twelve shared blocks across `PUSH-AUDIT.md` and `PLAN-TEMPLATE.md`
diff clean against `shakenfist/development`.

Not verifiable off-runner, and the reason to watch this PR's first run:
the gitleaks download on `[self-hosted, static]`, the `stbenjam/skillsaw@v0`
action, and the re-review lane, which only exercises on a real comment.

### TypeScript Migration and Type Safety

body:
Completes the platform's flagship: **correlation across different data types**. Links a graph `Entity` (narrative, from document NER) to a shared `Signal` (quantitative, from the temporal correlator) with a `HAS_SIGNAL` edge when they name the same concept.

## Change
- **`core/correlation/entity_signal.py`**: `EntitySignalCorrelator` matches an entity's own text **or its `SAME_AS`-resolved aliases** (slice 4.3) against a `Signal`'s tag (normalized), then `MERGE (Entity)-[:HAS_SIGNAL {method,owner_id}]->(Signal)`. Entities are per-user; Signals are shared → the edge is owned by the entity's owner. No new backend (reads existing Entity + Signal nodes). Registered unconditionally.

This makes the full cross-modal traversal work:
```
Entity -HAS_SIGNAL-> Signal -CORRELATES_WITH-> Signal <-HAS_SIGNAL- Entity
```
i.e. **"which entities' quantitative signals move together"** — the narrative↔quantitative bridge, the heart of the correlation vision.

## Testing
- Full suite **2924 passed**; lint (+ standalone `isort`) + mypy clean.
- Unit tests: exact match, `SAME_AS`-alias match, no-signals / no-match no-op, engine registration.
- **Live-verified end-to-end**: entity `BTC-USD` → `HAS_SIGNAL` → `Signal(crypto_price:BTC-USD)` `-CORRELATES_WITH->` `Signal(ETH-USD)`, coef=1.0.

## Phase 4 status — correlation engine COMPLETE (5 correlators)
co-occurrence · embedding-neighbour · entity-resolution · temporal (signal↔signal) · **entity↔signal**. Cross-modal correlation vision works e2e.

**Follow-on (documented):** embedding/fuzzy entity↔signal matching ("Bitcoin"↔BTC-USD without an exact alias); **scalability** — the embedding/temporal/entity-signal passes are O(n²) pure-Python (fine per-tenant; a Neo4j vector index / DB-side aggregation is needed for very-large-scale corpora); and the deferred Phase-2 `ai.py`→orchestration-service extraction.

body:
Alliance 6.0-A, LOT-06 — **dernier lot de la campagne**. Le patient voit son
dossier d'ensemble au portail et peut répondre à l'objectif négocié avec son
praticien : « c'est bien ça » ou « ce n'est pas exactement ça ».

**Aucune migration** : les cinq tables sont en production depuis le LOT-01.
`schema.prisma`, `prisma/migrations/` et `prisma/checks/` ne sont pas dans le
diff — la dérive schéma ↔ migrations est vérifiée nulle au T3.

## Le cadrage a corrigé trois affirmations du fichier de lot

1. **« Assembler les objets (lecture) » supposait trois lectures patient ; il en
   existait UNE.** L'objectif négocié n'était servi qu'au cockpit praticien, et
   le GET d'`api/portail/ce-qui-compte` n'est qu'un interrupteur — le patient ne
   pouvait pas relire ce qu'il avait déposé. Le lot **ouvre**, il n'assemble pas.
2. **« Visibilité praticien de l'état de ratification » était DÉJÀ LIVRÉE** au
   LOT-02. Il n'en restait qu'un libellé à réviser.
3. **« Le chemin est déjà inscrit par le LOT-04 » est FAUX** : servir la
   reformulation du praticien au patient est un chemin sortant **neuf**. Une
   garde vit dans un appelant, pas dans un objet.

## Le contrat

- **La ratification est un geste du patient, et elle a désormais un lieu
  unique.** Le LOT-02 interdisait TOUTE écriture, `create` compris, pour
  qu'aucune route praticien ne fabrique un acte que le patient n'a pas posé.
  Cette garde ne s'est pas ouverte : elle s'est **déplacée**, épinglée
  nommément sur la route portail écrivante. Ajouter une exception aurait fait
  dire à l'interdit « sauf là où quelqu'un a écrit ».
- **Répondre ne se retire pas.** Se raviser, c'est répondre à nouveau : une
  ligne de plus, et c'est le **dernier geste** qui vaut — jamais une majorité,
  jamais un décompte (`DC-30`). Aucun verbe n'existe pour effacer un accord
  donné, ni dans la route ni à l'écran.
- **Aucune date n'est écrite par l'application.** `cree_le` vient de la base ;
  `geste_le` reste **nulle** — c'est une colonne de DÉCLARATION, or le patient
  ne déclare rien, il clique. La renseigner depuis l'horloge du serveur en
  ferait une déclaration qu'il n'a pas faite, et elle ne pourrait jamais
  différer de `cree_le` : cette route est le seul écrivain.
- **Deux têtes d'objectif ⇒ aucune ratification proposée**, 409 même quand le
  patient vise la plus récente. Ratifier « la plus récente » trancherait en
  silence une discordance que `DC-30` demande de signaler.
- **`id_objectif` n'a pas de clé étrangère** (référence souple assumée par la
  migration) : trois contrôles à la route — existe, appartient au dossier, est
  la tête unique. 404 **indifférencié** entre « inexistant » et « d'un autre
  dossier », pas d'oracle d'existence.

## Le drapeau, et pourquoi il est neuf

`WN_DOSSIER_DEUX_VOIX`, quatrième de la campagne, fail-closed. Il garde la
route (503), l'écran (404) et **la ratification** (503). Il ne se compose pas
des deux existants : les réutiliser aurait ouvert la seule écriture patient
irréversible de la campagne du même geste qui ouvre une lecture — et l'objectif
négocié, lui, n'a aucun drapeau du tout.

Chaque bloc reste soumis au sien, et **un bloc fermé est ABSENT** — pas vide,
pas « pas encore ouvert » : l'un parlerait au patient d'un déploiement, l'autre
lui ferait lire un silence de son praticien (`DC-24`).

## Le sixième chemin de la carte du Socle — TROIS textes, pas deux

Régime **journalisant**, par application de `D-090` (le geste est un service).
La revue a trouvé que `priorite` — libellé libre du praticien, servi au patient
— en était absente alors que la carte promettait le contraire : une garde qui
n'énumère pas tous les champs d'un objet laisse le champ oublié hors du chemin
qu'elle prétend couvrir.

## TROIS mutations, vues rouges puis rebranchées vertes

| Mutation | Banc | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| garde de registre → `if (false)` | `api/portail/dossier/route.test.ts` | **rouge** (3) |
| `ratificationObjectif.create` → `.upsert` | `objectifNegocie.guard.test.ts` | **rouge** (2) |
| `{ceQuiCompte.length}` ajouté à l'écran | `ceQuiCompteAntiAgregat.guard.test.ts` | **rouge** (1) |

La troisième mérite son motif : le détecteur était lié au **nom** `entrees` et
laissait donc passer `{ceQuiCompte.length}`. La garde tenait par le nom que
l'auteur avait choisi, c'est-à-dire par rien. Généralisée, avec **une exception
nommée** — le compteur de caractères d'un champ de saisie.

## Revue

`wn-reviewer` a rendu **NO-GO**. Deux bloquants, refermés.

1. **Le premier cas E2E échouait de façon déterministe** (trouvé aussi par T2
   avant lecture de la revue) : le hub rend « Avant de commencer » avant tout le
   reste ; tant que la séquence n'est pas franchie, la nav n'existe pas dans le
   DOM. Le banc mesurait l'absence du gate, pas celle du lien.
2. **L'écran comblait deux dates que personne n'avait déclarées** :
   `saisiLe ?? creeLe` en tête de la parole du patient, et « Écrit le » sur une
   date de *publication*. La route déclare pourtant « jamais comblée », et le
   LOT-03 l'avait écrit : « ici **ni à l'affichage** ». Le cockpit praticien
   respectait la règle, l'écran patient faisait l'inverse — deux absences
   rendues comme des réponses (`DC-24`), sur la surface la plus exposée.

Quatre majeurs traités : `priorite` hors garde (ci-dessus) ; les **désaccords**
lus, transportés au navigateur et jamais affichés — un patient ayant contesté au
LOT-04 ne le voyait nulle part, et « Répondre à ce texte » lui parlait comme
s'il n'avait rien dit ; le libellé du cockpit, dont les deux formulations
évidentes étaient fausses, chacune dans une position du drapeau ; la garde
anti-agrégat qui ne couvrait pas l'écran.

Et **une question de la revue a changé le modèle** : quel usage `gesteLe` a-t-il
que `creeLe` ne couvre pas ? Aucun — elle est devenue nulle.

## RISQUES

- **Le drapeau est neuf et éteint.** Borné par : fail-closed sur la chaîne
  exacte `'true'`, gardant les trois gestes ; aucun bloc n'est servi sans son
  propre drapeau ; l'ouverture reste un geste du responsable, et poser la
  variable ne suffit pas — il faut un build qui la porte (piège `D-071`).
- **La ratification est irréversible et sans cadence.** Bornée par : append-only
  assumé (aucun verbe d'effacement n'existe), écrivain unique épinglé par garde
  structurelle vue rouge, `idPatient` issu de la session seule, aucune date
  écrite par l'application. **Non borné : le volume** — aucune limitation de
  fréquence, même régime qu'au LOT-03, mais c'est la première écriture
  *irréversible* de la campagne.
- **`id_objectif` n'a pas de clé étrangère.** Borné par les trois contrôles en
  route et le 404 indistinct. Résiduel : une reformulation concurrente entre le
  contrôle et l'insertion — visible (409), jamais silencieuse.
- **Un chemin sortant neuf sert au patient du texte écrit par le praticien.**
  Borné par la re-vérification au service sur les trois textes, régime
  journalisant, banc de débranchement vu rouge.
- **Trois surfaces patient couvertes par un E2E pour la première fois.** Bornée
  par : drapeaux armés aux trois endroits requis, fixtures des cinq tables,
  nettoyage ajouté à `resetPortailState` (qui les ignorait). Non couvert : la
  position **drapeau éteint**, non jouable dans le même run (les drapeaux sont
  armés au build).
- **Rien ne prévient le praticien qu'une ratification est arrivée** — le modèle
  « pull » assumé côté patient s'applique ici au praticien. Surface non cadrée.
- **`messageJournalisable` est désormais dupliqué dans trois routes.** Dette
  nommée, non factorisée dans ce lot.
- **`D-092` : le gate se constate sur la structure.** Borné par : le constat
  exige `scalingo run -d` (le MCP lit la base gelée depuis le cutover) et ne
  pose ni drapeau ni activation élargie. **La lecture elle-même reste DUE** — le
  CLI Scalingo exige un login du responsable, et `D-092` porte ce reste
  explicitement plutôt que de l'énoncer au passé.

## Validation

- **T3 complet vert** (exit 0) : 5 495 Vitest sur 442

body:
### Stack

This is part of a four-PR chain. Each branch builds on the previous one; please review in order.

| | PR | Branch | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | this one | `feat/league-alias-foundations` | Alias parsing, league alias persistence, unified league identity, token catalog |
| 2 | #___ | `feat/league-alias-query-plan` | Structured query plan, bounded league-alias expansion |
| 3 | #___ | `feat/per-indexer-search-cache` | Per-indexer result caching, full plan execution, opt-in strong-match stop |
| 4 | #___ | `feat/advanced-league-search-settings` | Advanced Search Settings UI, structured preview, docs |

**← You are here: PR 1.**

## Why

Sportarr already accepts several alternate league and team names when *matching* releases, but its indexer queries use a smaller, partly hardcoded set. A release can therefore be matchable but undiscoverable. This PR lays the foundation for fixing that: it gives leagues a durable local alias field and makes every league-identity check read from one enumeration.

It also fixes a bug that exists today, independent of any of the above: `PUT /api/teams/{id}/aliases` splits on comma alone, so pipe- and slash-separated input ("Man Utd | MUFC") is stored as a single alias and never matches anything.

## What changed

- **One alias parser.** New `AliasField` helper parses comma, pipe, and slash separators with trimming and case-insensitive deduplication, and normalizes to a stable storage form. Both league and team alias writes go through it. Values over 512 characters are rejected with a field-specific 400 rather than truncated.
- **Three new local-only `League` columns**, all nullable with no backfill: `UserAliases`, a typed JSON `AliasSearchOrder`, and `SearchEarlyStopMatchScoreOverride`. Local-only means the weekly metadata refresh never writes them — that is the whole reason they cannot live in `AlternateName`. Migrations for both SQLite and PostgreSQL, plus the legacy `EnsureCreated` startup safety net.
- **One league-identity enumeration.** `LeagueAliasHelper.GetMatchingAliases` returns name, upstream aliases, user aliases, and generated abbreviations, deduplicated. Every identity path now uses it — organization validation, `TitleNamesLeague`, `SeriesLabelMatchesLeague`, grab validation, import matching. The private duplicate list that knew only about `Name` and `AlternateName` is deleted.
- **Authoritative token catalog.** `BuildQueryFromTemplate` supports 19 tokens, the frontend showed 16, and the backend endpoint returned 12. All three now agree on the same 19, with a key-parity test. `{Round:00}`, `{Stage:0}`, and `{vs}` become insertable from the UI for the first time.

## Why the identity change is a correctness requirement, not a nicety

A release found through a user alias must not then fail league-identity matching because the matcher does not know that alias. Adding the alias to query generation without adding it to matching would produce results that get found and then rejected. That is why identity lands here, in the same PR as the field, rather than later with the query work.

## Not in this PR

No change to query generation, search execution, or caching. Aliases are stored and honored by the matcher; PR 2 starts searching for them.

`AliasSearchOrder` and `SearchEarlyStopMatchScoreOverride` are persisted and round-trip through the API, but nothing reads them yet — they are consumed by PRs 2 and 3. That is deliberate, not dead code.

## Testing

- Parser: separators, trimming, empties, case-insensitive dedupe.
- Round-trip of all three fields through add, get, and update.
- Metadata refresh changes `AlternateName` and leaves all three local values untouched.
- A title containing only a league user alias passes every applicable identity gate.
- Token metadata keys and replacement keys are exactly equal and cover all 19 tokens; frontend fallback matches literally.
- SQLite migration applies cleanly; legacy `EnsureCreated` startup is idempotent across two consecutive boots (boot 2 is a verified no-op — no re-add, no errors).
- Full backend suite: **1345/1345 passing**.
- Frontend lint is **byte-identical to the `dev` baseline** (252 problems / 209 errors / 43 warnings on both sides, verified by line-level diff against a clean merge-base worktree — this branch adds zero). Build clean. The frontend suite has 7 pre-existing failures (`AddEventModal.test.tsx` ×4, `useSettings.test.ts` ×3), independently confirmed present at the merge base; this branch touches neither file and adds 4 passing tests.

## ⚠️ One validation gap the author could not close

**The PostgreSQL migration has never been executed.** It was generated by real `dotnet ef` tooling and its contents were verified by reading — `AddColumn` for all three columns as nullable `text`/`text`/`integer`, no `defaultValue`, no backfill, `Down` drops all three — but the development environment had no PostgreSQL server, no `psql` client, and no reachable Docker daemon, so `migrations add` could be run while `database update` could not.

The SQLite path *was* exercised end to end, including the legacy-schema safety net across two boots.

Please run this migration against a real Postgres instance (CI or a local container) before merging, or treat that as a release gate. If it were wrong, the failure mode is a broken startup for every Postgres-backed deployment on upgrade.

## Review focus

The identity enumeration adoption in `ReleaseMatchingService` and `LibraryImportService` — confirm no second league-alias list survives anywhere.

Two deliberate decisions worth a second opinion:

- **`LibraryImportService`'s organization gate is now more permissive.** It previously compared against `League.Name` only; it now checks every alias. This is monotonic — `GetMatchingAliases` always returns the canonical name first, so every string that matched before still matches — but it is a hard gate becoming looser and deserves a look.
- **EPG channel-to-league auto-mapping deliberately does *not* honor `UserAliases`.** It now uses the shared parser so there is one parser in the codebase, but still reads only `Name` + `AlternateName`, with a comment explaining why. Changing which channels auto-map is a product decision, deliberately excluded here.

## Known follow-ups (none blocking)

- No relational round-trip test opening real SQLite to read `AliasSearchOrder` back; the JSON conversion is asserted in memory.
- `PUT /api/teams/{id}/aliases` is an inline lambda with no testable seam, so its 400 length-cap branch, JSON parsing, and analytics side effect remain uncovered at the endpoint level. The shared `AliasField` logic it delegates to *is* covered. Extracting a helper purely for testability was judged out of scope.
- `LeagueAliasHelper` has no direct unit tests; it is covered through its four call sites.
- Migration timestamps are EF-generated (`20260822174658`, `20260822174711`) rather than the plan's placeholder values.
- The plan called for `ILogger<LeagueEndpoints>` on the token endpoint; `LeagueEndpoints` is a static class, so that does not compile (CS0718). `ILogger<Program>` was kept, matching the existing `SonarrQueueEndpoints` precedent.

author: wshlavacek
body:
Fixes #642.

## What was wrong

On a cluster where `salloc` returns a shell on the **login node** while the allocation is held on a compute node — which is the shell PyBNF is meant to run in, since it is the one that holds the allocation — the `srun` launcher stopped before a single worker started:

    srun: error: Unable to create step for job NNNNN: More processors requested than permitted

`Cluster.cpus_per_node` prefers `$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE`, which SLURM sets only inside a job step running on an allocated node. On the login node it is simply absent, so the count fell through to `dask.system.CPU_COUNT` and then to the machine's processor count — both of which describe the login node, which is not in the allocation and is usually several times larger than what the job holds. A job granted 20 CPUs was sized as though it held 128, and `--cpus-per-task 128` is a request SLURM refuses outright.

## The fix

Two parts, both in `pybnf/cluster.py`. ADR-0125 records the reasoning.

**1. The job's own per-node list is a source of the single count.** `cpus_per_node` now consults `$SLURM_JOB_CPUS_PER_NODE` — the per-node list SLURM publishes for the **job**, which is set correctly in a login-node shell — between `$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE` and the two machine-level numbers. Its smallest entry is taken, because this single number both sizes a pool started on every machine and is what one `srun` step asks for on every machine in it: asking for less than a machine holds costs speed, asking for more than the smallest holds is refused. Inside the allocation nothing changes — `$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE` is still preferred where SLURM sets it. This also fixes the same login-node exposure on the SSH launcher (`-t slurm`), which reads the same count.

**2. The layout hands its counts on rather than having them re-derived** (the fix suggested in the issue). `srun_worker_layout` already reads the per-node list before choosing which command to build; the equal-size path now passes that count — and the phrase naming its source, for the log — into `srun_worker_command`, which derives one itself only when no caller supplied it. So a `$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE` that does not describe this job, including one exported by hand as the workaround for this bug, no longer sizes a later run.

The `srun` argument list is otherwise untouched: a launch from inside the allocation builds the command it built before, and the existing regression test that pins that argv still passes.

## Verification

The constructed `srun` argument list is the oracle, as it was for #614 and #617. Eight new tests; all seven that target the defect fail on `main` and pass here:

* `cpus_per_node` — the job list is read when the step variable is empty; a mixed list reduces to its smallest machine; the step variable still wins when both are set; an unreadable or zero list falls through to the local numbers.
* `srun_worker_command` — a caller-supplied count is used instead of the environment (and its source reaches the log); it still caps an oversubscribed `parallel_count`.
* `setup_srun_cluster`, end to end in a stood-up login-node environment (no `$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE`, a job list of 20, machine-level numbers of 128) — the default path asks for 20 workers and 20 CPUs rather than 128; an explicit `parallel_count = 64` starts all 64 workers but asks for 20 CPUs, so the step is not refused; and the count the layout read is the count the command uses even when `$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE` is stale.
* `per_node_cpus` — the two fixes compose: a list that cannot be lined up with the machines still supplies the fallback count rather than the login node's size.

Full local gate green (4564 passed) apart from one unrelated pre-existing failure — `test_gradient_sens_fallback.py::test_a_declined_model_is_reported_identically_cold_and_warm`, which fails on a clean `main` too against a bngsim built from upstream main and is filed as #644. Docs updated (`docs/cluster.rst`, `docs/config_keys.rst`) and a CHANGELOG entry added.

## Also noted

ADR-0124 recorded a limitation on the `parallel_count` path — on a mixed-size allocation its even split can ask for more CPUs than the smallest machine holds — and asked for its own tracking issue rather than being folded into that change. That is now filed as #643, and this PR deliberately leaves it alone: what changed here is only that the single count it is capped by describes the allocation rather than the machine PyBNF is launched from.

body:
This adds the first deliberately narrow RGBX v2 host ABI slice behind a second default-off config: numeric parameters, ordered eight-pixel spans, and a `cpptest` conformance guest.

## What changes

- Add exact `rgbx_v2.param_u32(i32) -> i32` and `rgbx_v2.set_span8(...) -> void` imports.
- Require exact `rgbx_init() -> void` and `rgbx_tick(i32) -> void` exports, reject imported globals and cross-profile modules, and bound functions, globals, locals, parameter calls, and span calls.
- Commit a frame only after exactly 60 ordered spans cover all 480 pixels; traps and rejected host calls leave caller output unchanged.
- Port `cpptest` as a memoryless guest and compare every output pixel across state and parameter changes.

## Validation

- ARM QEMU: 25/25 runtime and v2 ABI cases pass with no warnings, including host-call quotas, wrong span order, incomplete frames, missing or malformed exports, wrong import signatures, imported globals, admission-budget abort, profile separation, atomic output, and recovery.
- Explicit proto0 build with both default-off configs enabled succeeds and compiles the v2 entry points.
- That build uses 842,192 of 900,608 flash bytes and 434,176 of 450,560 RAM bytes, below both stop-loss margins; no board enables it and no device was flashed.
- Default firmware still excludes the Wasm runtime.
- Independent code and security review is green; privacy and secret scans are clean.

Sensors, retained frames, guest linear memory, community effects, package loading, runtime selection, and LLEXT removal remain separate later layers.
The checked Wasm module is explicitly a reviewed behavioral fixture; reproducible source-to-artifact compiler provenance is a separate compiler-fixture gate.

This extends our usage of EC2 to dist-x86_64-linux-alt builders (1h23m with m8a.2xlarge, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/actions/runs/32137297331/job/95711706485).

This is moving from GHA credits to EC2 credits, so we should confirm we want that, but in dollar terms this is cheaper: at 1h55m (last auto build) on [GHA $1.32/hr](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing) = $2.53/run, vs. 1h23m on EC2 at $0.48688/hr = $0.67/run.

My primary goal is to try to free up GHA credits so we can move Windows and/or macOS jobs to large runners, since I suspect us trying to host those ourselves is going to be more painful.

As a drive-by change this also adds support for EC2 aarch64 machines to the bors config (but not CI config). My suspicion is that if/when we have aarch64 perf we may want faster aarch64 try builds, and in any case dist-aarch64-linux is one of our slower runners -- at 2h24m -- so it may benefit from getting a faster machine. I don't know yet how EC2 will compare but extending the bors config is cheap so I'd rather just do that now to enable easier testing.

I also deleted some of the old unused runner templates, I don't see much point in keeping dead ones around.

## Summary

`ATrooperEnemy` was the only concrete `AEnemyBase` subclass that never constructed a `UEnemyTypeIndicatorComponent`. Since PR #212 made `ATargetZone::HandleZoneOverlap`'s acceptance type-keyed (`FindComponentByClass<UEnemyTypeIndicatorComponent>()`), a Controlled Trooper arriving at any type-keyed pen always resolved to `nullptr` and was rejected outright — making any level containing a Trooper unclearable. The same missing component also meant Troopers showed no floating type-codename marker in PIE, unlike the other three core enemy types (Bomber, Runner, Sniper).

**Root cause**: PR #131 added `ATrooperEnemy` mirroring `ASniperEnemy`/`ABomberEnemy`'s mesh+glow+tell+telegraph shape, 5 days before `UEnemyTypeIndicatorComponent` even existed (issue #77, same day). `ARunnerEnemy`, implemented afterward, picked the component up correctly; `ATrooperEnemy` was never retrofitted. The gap was purely cosmetic until PR #212 made the component load-bearing for banking.

## Changes

- `TrooperEnemy.h` — forward-declare `UEnemyTypeIndicatorComponent`, add the `TObjectPtr<UEnemyTypeIndicatorComponent> EnemyTypeIndicatorComponent` property (matches `RunnerEnemy.h`/`BomberEnemy.h`/`SniperEnemy.h`'s declaration shape exactly).
- `TrooperEnemy.cpp` — construct the component in the constructor and set `EnemyType = EEnemyType::TR_UPR`, mirroring the identical pattern in the three sibling classes.
- `KrowdKontrolEnemyTypeIndicatorComponentTest.cpp` — extend part (a) to check the real `ARunnerEnemy`/`ATrooperEnemy` classes (previously only `ABomberEnemy`/`ASniperEnemy` were checked against real actors; Runner/Trooper coverage was via synthetic stand-ins that couldn't have caught this bug).
- `KrowdKontrolRoomActorBankingWiringTest.cpp` — add a third marker/zone (TR_UPR) and a positive scenario: a Controlled Trooper delivered onto its own type-matched zone reaches `Banked`. Per the issue's explicit acceptance criterion.

Per this repo's `app-source-tracked/` convention (CLAUDE.md), the real edits live in the gitignored `app/` Unreal project; this PR's diff is a plain-text mirror of those same four files under `app-source-tracked/Source/KrowdKontrol/...` for reviewability. `app/`'s live copies were confirmed byte-identical to the mirrors during validation.

## Deviation from plan

`ARoomActor::AddTargetZone()` attaches every marker to the room's own actor location (no per-marker placement param), so the new `TrooperMarker` and its zone would have spatially overlapped the existing "wrong-type" rejection fixture's zone, causing a false pass/fail interaction (first harness run caught this: the mismatched Trooper incorrectly banked at the wrong zone). Fixed by explicitly moving `TrooperMarker` to `(5000, 5000, 0)` after spawning, clear of the other two zones. Not called out in the original investigation/plan.

## Validation

- `python harness/ci.py` (full mode): `UE_AUTOMATION_RESULT passed=92 total=93`, one failure — `KrowdKontrol.Unit.PlayerControllerShowsMouseCursor`.
  - Confirmed **unrelated**: that test lives in `KrowdKontrolCursorWorldPositionTest.cpp`, which this branch never touches. It was added on a different, still-unmerged branch (`archon/task-fix-issue-262`) that shares the same `app/` symlink in this factory's worktree setup (`FACTORY_RULES.md` §8 concurrency caveat), so its in-progress work is currently visible to this branch's build/test pass. Not a regression introduced here.
- Hard invariants: pass. Diff only adds the existing `UEnemyTypeIndicatorComponent` (already used by all other enemy types) to `ATrooperEnemy`, set to the existing, locked `TR_UPR` enum value — no new colour (Invariant #3), no new enemy type (Invariant #5).
- Scope check: no protected files touched (no `MISSION.md`/`FACTORY_RULES.md`/`CLAUDE.md`/`.github/`/deploy config).

Manual PIE verification (per investigation.md, not run in this automated pass):
1. A Trooper should now show a floating "TR-UPR" text marker.
2. A Controlled Trooper delivered to a type-matched pen should reach `Banked`.
3. Runner/Bomber/Sniper banking is unaffected (covered by existing automation).

## Known follow-up (flagged, not fixed here — out of scope)

`EnemyTypeIndicatorComponent.cpp`'s marker-rotation logic assumes the owner's root component has identity world rotation, which is true for every other enemy type but not `ATrooperEnemy` (90° root Roll). This fix is the first trigger for that pre-existing comment: the "TR-UPR" marker text will likely render sideways rather than upright for Troopers specifically. This doesn't block banking (Roll doesn't affect which side faces the camera) and isn't part of this issue's root cause or acceptance criteria — flagging as a suggested fast-follow if PIE QA finds it objectionable.

Fixes #242

author: marekgrzeska
body:
Three things on the Strategie tab from #212. Reported from the deployed terminal: clicking **Zacznij** did nothing.

## The button was disabled, and could not stop being

`StartWatchDialog` kept the chosen strategy as a `useState` **initial value**:

```tsx
const [strategyId, setStrategyId] = useState(strategies[0]?.id ?? "");
```

Open the dialog before the catalogue answers — seconds, against a cold App Service — and that state is `""` for good. The select fills itself afterwards, but a controlled `<select value="">` matches no option, so nothing is selected, `confirmDisabled` stays true, and the operator clicks a dead button with nothing on screen explaining it.

The choice is derived now — `chosen ?? strategies[0]?.id ?? ""`, where `null` means "not chosen yet" — so the first entry becomes the selection the moment the catalogue lands. An empty catalogue says so in the dialog instead of leaving a dead button to say it.

This is not an authorization problem: `REST_CALLER_APPLICATION_IDS` on the strategy app, the `preAuthorizedApplications` entry on `api://tradingcenter-strategy` and `VITE_ENTRA_SCOPE_STRATEGY` in the deployed bundle were all checked against Azure and are in place.

## The instrument is picked, not typed

A strategy decides on the archive's candles and on nothing else, so a symbol the archive does not collect is a watch that can only ever record refusals — and typed by hand, its spelling is a guess the operator cannot check from the dialog. It is a select over what the archive is collecting, read when the dialog opens rather than with the screen: one request, wanted only by somebody about to start something.

What the archive holds for the chosen instrument is shown beside it, in the terminal's own interval names — including the strategy's own, which used to reach the screen as the wire's `HOUR`. Shown rather than checked against it: which interval can be served from which is the archive's rule (a rollup is built off the minute series), and a copy of it here would be a second opinion that drifts. The platform records a coverage refusal, with its reason, when the bars are not there.

## The screen had no styles

It named eleven classes — `chip`, `chip-on`, `watch`, `watch-on`, `watch-symbol`, `watch-strategy`, `decisions`, `decision`, `decision-*`, `badge`, `kind-*` — and `index.css` defined none of them; Tailwind v4 generates no such utilities. The filter row, the watched pairs and the whole table of decisions rendered unstyled.

They are written as rules on the tokens rather than as utilities on the elements: the vocabulary repeats on every row, and the three kinds of refusal are the one place colour carries meaning — `coverage` is the only kind that means something is missing (warning), `limit` is amber because a person raises it, `strategy` is steel because the platform declining a bar is the ordinary state.

## Tests

Starting a watch had no test at all. Four now: what the archive offers and the pair that was picked, the regression above (catalogue arriving after the dialog), a refusal from the module kept beside the question it answers, and an archive collecting nothing. The regression test fails on the old code and passes on the new.

`vitest` 789 passed · `tsc` clean · `eslint` clean · `vite build` clean.

Not an OpenSpec change: no requirement, contract or infrastructure moves — `terminal-strategy` already asks for this, it was simply not delivered.

body:
Bakes a Draft-PR/progress-ledger workflow into the cc-rc image, so every headless coding-task agent creates a branch, opens a Draft PR, and keeps its progress in the PR description before/while it works — resumable by a fresh agent if the session is lost. Also adds a sized `emptyDir` at `/tmp` on the agent container.

<details>
<summary>Plan</summary>

# Bake a git/PR workflow into the cc-rc image

## Context

`cc-rc` runs headless Claude Code agents (`claude remote-control --spawn worktree`) in Kubernetes pods that can be killed/rescheduled at any time. Push (SSH deploy key) and `gh` (via `GH_TOKEN`) are already fully wired and authenticated in every pod, but nothing told an agent how to use them. If a session was lost mid-task, there was no branch, no PR, and no record of progress for a fresh agent to resume from.

The goal: bake in instructions (a user-level `CLAUDE.md`) plus a small helper tool, so every agent, on every repo it works in, creates a branch and opens a Draft PR before writing code (an early smoke test that push/`gh` access work), keeps a progress ledger in the PR description written for a future agent rather than a human, commits with Conventional Commits, and marks the PR ready for review once its plan is done.

## Changes

1. New `.claude/CLAUDE.md` — user-level workflow instructions, baked into the image at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
2. New `scripts/cc-rc-pr-update.sh` — agent-facing helper installed to `~/.local/bin/cc-rc-pr-update`, so the agent never hand-crafts PR markdown or juggles create-vs-edit itself. The Plan and Progress ledger sections both render collapsed.
3. `Dockerfile` — two more bind mounts in the existing `setup-dev.sh` layer.
4. `scripts/setup-dev.sh` — copies/installs both new files.
5. `README.md` — documents the new baked-in workflow.
6. Chart: explicit sized `emptyDir` at `/tmp` on the agent container (`storage.tmpSize`, default `2Gi`), since `cc-rc-pr-update` and the agent's own work write temp files there and nothing backs `/tmp` explicitly today.

## Verification

CI (`Docker Build and Push`, `Helm`) is green on this PR, `helm unittest charts/cc-rc` passes 83/83, and the built `pr-10` image was inspected directly (via `crane export`, no local Docker in this environment) to confirm `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and `~/.local/bin/cc-rc-pr-update` landed correctly and `cc-rc-pr-update` resolves on `PATH`.

author: bradysox
body:
Two faults in the naval branch of `TheaterUnit.kill`, both shipped, one of which reaches the supercarriers.

## 1. Every helicopter carrier was exempt from its own sinking

The grounding matched `UnitClass.AIRCRAFT_CARRIER` alone. Six hulls are classed `HELICOPTER_CARRIER` and kept their air wing after going under:

`Essex` · `LHA_Tarawa` · `Hms_invincible` · `L02` · `L61` · `Type_071`

The Essex is the sharp case. It carries that class **deliberately** — it is the condition `start_generator.transform_to_essex_if_needed` tests before swapping the control point for `EssexCarrier`, which subclasses `Carrier` and gates basing on `lha_capable` because a 1944 deck has no catapults. So a ship pydcs reports at `plane_num=90, helicopter_num=1` was exempt from its own sinking. For contrast, LHA-1 Tarawa is 40 and 36.

**Do not "fix" this by reclassifying `Essex.yaml`.** That would break the transform. The fix belongs in the kill branch, which is where it is.

## 2. Squadrons were removed while the list holding them was being walked

`ControlPoint.squadrons` is a generator:

```python
for squadron in self.coalition.air_wing.iter_squadrons():
    if squadron.location == self:
        yield squadron
```

and `AirWing.iter_squadrons` is `itertools.chain.from_iterable(self.squadrons.values())` — a lazy chain over the live lists. The loop body removed from those same lists, so elements were skipped: with two squadrons of one aircraft type on a hull, **the second survived**.

This one is not about classification. It hits a correctly-classed CVN today.

## The fix

```python
 if (
     unit.unit_type
-    and unit.unit_type.unit_class is UnitClass.AIRCRAFT_CARRIER
+    and unit.unit_type.unit_class
+    in (UnitClass.AIRCRAFT_CARRIER, UnitClass.HELICOPTER_CARRIER)
     and not unit.alive
 ):
     cp = self.ground_object.control_point
-    for squadron in cp.squadrons:
+    for squadron in list(cp.squadrons):
```

## The test

`tests/theater/test_carrier_sinking.py`, 6 cases. Two decisions worth flagging to a reviewer:

- **The fakes reuse the real `AirWing.iter_squadrons` and the real `ControlPoint.squadrons` property** rather than re-implementing them. The lazy iteration *is* the second fault, so a faked iterator would prove nothing. `AirWing.__init__` wants a `Game` and a `Faction` to build squadron defs, none of it reachable from `kill()`, so the wing is built with `object.__new__` and only `squadrons` populated.
- **Ship types are the real DCS ones**, and each parametrised case asserts the hull's `unit_class` before exercising behaviour. Reclassify `Essex.yaml` and the test says so, instead of the behaviour changing quietly.

Coverage: a supercarrier (baseline, passed before this change), the Essex, an LHA, two squadrons sharing an aircraft type, an escort sinking under a carrier that is still afloat, and squadrons at other bases being left alone.

Before the fix: 4 failed, 2 passed. After: 6 passed.

## Verification

Black clean · mypy clean on 960 source files · **4316 passed, 10 skipped**.

Changelog and `whatsnew.yaml` entries included — the bug shipped, so it is player-visible.

## Provenance

Found while checking whether the Marianas 1944 Essex could base aircraft for #944. It can. This is the separate defect that turned up alongside, and it is deliberately not in that PR.

author: vassilatanasov
body:
Three commits, all aimed at the same thing: Ivan finishing a feature unattended without either lying about quality or paging a human over something routine.

## Adopt to the target project's stack, and finish the ADO port (cb1562a)

`/adopt` now settles the stack **once**, up front — new section 3 detects it from the repo, confirms it with the user detected-answer-first, and records six lines in the Ivan project config (`Stack`, `Layout`, `App shape`, `Run commands`, `QA tooling`, `Supply chain`). Everything stack-dependent reads that record instead of re-deriving it. An undecided stack defers the dependent sections to `/discover` rather than being guessed: a gate built for the wrong stack passes trivially forever while every later phase believes it is protected.

- **`gate.ps1` gains a Python leg** (ruff format/check, mypy or pyright picked from `[tool.pyright]`, pytest), so the Python conventions the plugin already shipped finally have enforcement.
- **Every leg ends in a supply-chain step** — `dotnet list package --vulnerable` parsed for High/Critical (it exits 0 whatever it finds), `npm audit --audit-level=high` which fails outright on a missing lockfile, `pip-audit --strict` which fails when the tool is absent rather than skipping in silence. An agent that adds dependencies unattended is exactly the case where a known-vulnerable package has to be a red build. `GATE_SKIP_SUPPLY_CHAIN` is offline-local only; the pipeline never sets it, so skipping locally still fails the branch policy.
- **New section 3d works out what the `qa-verifier` will need** from the app shape, installs it, records the per-component port override (two worktrees can verify at once), and proves it once with the user present. The agent now reads those config lines as authoritative instead of inferring a start command from source, and reports a missing tool rather than working around it — previously a silent hole, since `UNVERIFIABLE` is not a red build.
- **`azure-pipelines.yml` becomes profile-shaped**, under the rule that every step the local gate runs must be runnable on the agent — otherwise CI goes red for something the circuit breaker cannot tell apart from a real defect.
- Two hazards fixed in passing: `stop-gate.ps1` filtered changes on `server/|client/` and would have stopped firing the moment `/adopt` pointed the gate elsewhere (now an exclude list); `code-reviewer` diffed `main...HEAD`, but reviews run in a worktree branched off `origin/main` where local `main` may be stale or absent.
- The tail of the Azure DevOps port: the last Workflowy/GitHub references, a committed commit-message temp file, and two docs still describing the pre-PR world.

## Catch human-gated policies at adoption, and stop charging flaky builds (bc958ac)

`policy-check` at setup time, so a blocking policy only a person can satisfy is found with the user in the room instead of mid-autopilot; `build-triage` separates a failing build caused by our code from a dropped agent or dead feed, and only the former spends a circuit-breaker strike.

## Classify pr-wait outcomes so only real dead ends reach the user (7f176e5)

`pr-wait` exits with a code per outcome — merged, build rejected, conflicts, needs-a-human, abandoned, timed out — so a routine rebase behind another feature stops looking like a failure.

**The Cursor rail reported tokens it could not price, and could not say so.**

0.18.0 began metering Cursor turns. The model that prices them arrives on a

body:
## Why

The staging Azure OpenAI deployment (`gpt-4.1-mini`, GlobalStandard capacity 10 ≈ 10k TPM) cannot absorb a full 8-agent council (~48k tokens) fired back-to-back. The committee chair runs **last** and is the **largest** request (evidence pack + all prior summaries), so it repeatedly failed with `LLMRateLimitError` — reproduced 3× live. Its deterministic fallback then wrote `committee_label="insufficient_data"`, which **no downstream surface could distinguish from an evidence-based judgement**.

Separately, the company council's retry budgets (150s total / 45s reserve / 30s retry-after cap / 20s backoff cap) still encoded the **removed** synchronous ~230s-gateway constraint (dead since the async full-analysis job, PR #119). A ~48k-token council against a 10k-TPM deployment needs ≥5 minutes of refill windows — the old budgets made success mathematically impossible under throttling, and the 30s retry-after cap guaranteed the clamped retry fired back into the same exhausted window.

## What

1. **Async-era budgets** — company council 150→600s total, 45→180s reserve, 30→90s retry-after cap, 20→60s backoff cap; discovery + field-review caps raised in lockstep. Still strictly bounded; jobs always terminate.
2. **One shared token-pacing primitive** (`app/services/llm/token_pacer.py`) used by **all three councils** (mirrors how `retry_engine` is the one retry primitive): process-local sliding TPM window per (provider, deployment) — concurrent councils share one window — with an explicit **chair token reserve** non-chair agents cannot consume. **Advisory by design**: after a bounded wait the attempt always proceeds (provider 429 + bounded retries are the backstop), so imperfect estimates can never wedge a council or skip an agent. **Off by default** (`LLM_COUNCIL_TPM_CAPACITY=0`).
3. **Deterministic chair-input compaction** (`LLM_COUNCIL_CHAIR_PRIOR_SUMMARY_MAX_CHARS`, default 0 = off): truncated summary + cited evidence ids + top risks + unsupported-claim count per completed agent, failed agents named. Extraction only — never an LLM re-summarization, dissent never dropped.
4. **Failure-vs-judgement semantics (correctness)** — every council result persists `chair_synthesis_basis` (`"llm_chair"` = evidence-based, possibly after retries; `"deterministic_fallback"` = failure default), `chair_attempts`, `chair_error_type` (error class name only). Counts only — never prompts/completions/credentials.
6. **Coherent stale threshold** — `analysis_job_stale_after_minutes()` = max(configured base, derived council+pacing+ingestion worst case + margin); raising a council budget can never mark a legitimate long job stale mid-council.

Field-review's (pre-existing, engine-mirroring) retry loop is not ported onto `retry_engine.run_with_retries` — it shares the new pacing/usage primitives but keeps its validated loop. No durable queue. No Azure capacity change (separate human decision).

author: tsmith165
body:
Two things a staging business needs from this page that it could not do: see which finished jobs still owe money, and record a payment that arrived in two parts. This branch adds payment tracking and rebuilds the projects list around a persistent detail column.

## Payment is a record, not a flag

`projects` previously had one nullable `paymentReceivedAt`, which could answer "has any money arrived" and nothing else. It now carries a status, an amount, a method and a note alongside that date.

Toggling a project to paid opens a dialog rather than flipping a switch:

| Question | Why it's asked |
|---|---|
| In full, or part of it? | Deposit-then-balance is the normal shape of a staging invoice |
| Amount received | Reconciled against `revenue` to decide the real status |
| Date received | The day the money arrived, not the day the record was made |
| Method | Six one-tap options, free text otherwise, so records stay consistent |
| Notes | Check number, who paid |

On a project that is already part paid, the field asks for *this* payment and shows what has already been recorded, because that is what the cheque in hand says. The dialog states the consequence live — `$1,200.00 will still be outstanding` or `Recording $3,400.00 settles this job in full` — before anything is written.

**The amount is authoritative.** Entering the full invoice while `Part of it` is selected settles the job, because the number is a fact and the radio button is an intention. `recordProjectPayment` does that reconciliation server-side, so it holds regardless of which surface called it.

Legacy rows have no status. Every read goes through `paymentState`, which treats a pre-existing receipt date as paid in full — that was all the field could mean. Nothing needs backfilling.

The dashboard's awaiting-payment figure moves to `isAwaitingPayment`, so a partially-paid job now correctly reads as still outstanding instead of settled.

## The list gained a detail column

```
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ search + status/money filters│  selected        │
│ ────────────────────────────│  project         │
│ ▸ 123 Oak St  Active  Paid   │  facts, payment, │
│ ▸ 44 Elm      Done  $900 left│  quick edit,     │
│ ▸ 8 Pine      Draft          │  links, delete   │
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘
```

Above `xl` the column sits in the layout, so the list keeps scrolling behind it and there is no scrim to dismiss. Below `xl` the same body becomes a slide-over. That wrapper is now `AdminSidePanel`, shared with the inventory catalog rather than a second copy of it.

Rows carry what prompts action — status, payment with the outstanding balance, how many units are still at the house, photo count — so the two questions worth chasing are answerable without opening anything. The three trailing icon links are gone; those actions live in the detail column.

From the column: mark or clear payment, change name, status and revenue in place, or open the full project, its furniture, or its photos. A finished job with furniture still recorded on site says so and links to the check-in.

Selection is in the URL (`?project=…`), so a project can be linked to and returning from its editor lands on the same row.

Filters cover search, status and `Money owed` / `Settled`. Reorder arrows hide while a filter is active and the list says why — display order is global, so moving a row inside a filtered view moves it past projects that aren't on screen.

## On the project itself

Payment is a section of the project editor too, using the same dialog, and joins the jump nav. It is a step of its own rather than four more fields on the details form: it has its own date, its own reconciliation, and it is the one edit made months after everything else on the page has stopped changing.

## Incidental

`getAllProjects` and `getProjectById` move onto the `authz` helpers, replacing hand-rolled identity lookups. `getProjectsOverview` returns the list and its counts in one subscription. The old list's `as any` casts and leftover `console.log` reordering traces are gone.

author: danlesko
body:
Closes three type-safety boxes on #8. They are **one PR because they are atomic**: the lint rule cannot be enabled until both `any` sites are gone, so splitting them would mean a PR that cannot pass its own lint step.

## What changed

**`src/components/MyProcessingDrawing.tsx`** — deletes a double-cast: an inner `mod.ReactP5Wrapper as any` and an outer `as unknown as React.NamedExoticComponent<P5WrapperProps>`. Neither was needed — `dynamic` infers the props from the loader on its own — so the call is now just `dynamic(loader, { ssr: false })` and the `P5WrapperProps` import goes with them.

**`src/components/fishTankSketch.ts`** — the four `bColor` / `fColor` params on the two goldfish functions now take a named `P5Color` alias instead of `any`.

**`eslint.config.mjs`** — `"@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any": "off"` deleted, replaced by a comment saying why it must stay on.

## What the inner cast actually cost

Both casts were unsafe independently. The inner `as any` is why a loader resolving to the wrong export used to compile clean — that is the defect, and it is now caught. The outer `as unknown as` bypassed compatibility checking on the result outright, so it could have hidden a props mismatch too; it was never a check that the inner cast defeated.

My first commit here claimed something stronger and wrong — that `dynamic` *cannot* infer props through `ReactP5Wrapper`'s `MemoExoticComponent`, and that an explicit `dynamic<P5WrapperProps>` type argument was therefore required to drop the casts. Codex review challenged it and a probe disproved it: dropping the type argument typechecks clean and still catches the loader mutant. The second commit removes the unnecessary type argument and fixes the comment. Worth flagging because the false premise had produced real, unnecessary code — not just a wrong sentence.

## The p5 finding, which changes what this box could have been

**p5 1.11.8 ships no TypeScript declarations** — not one `.d.ts` in the package, no `types`/`typings` field, and `@types/p5` is not installed. Under `skipLibCheck` the p5 half of `P5CanvasInstance` degrades to `any`, so **there is no `Color` type to import**. The #8 box read as "swap `any` for the real type"; the real type does not exist here, and adding `@types/p5` is not available either — the registry in this environment 401s on new package fetches.

`type P5Color = unknown` is the most precise honest option and strictly better than the `any` it replaces: these values are only ever forwarded to `p5.fill()` — never read, indexed or mutated. The comment records the catch, which is that `unknown` is accepted there **only** because `fill` is reached through an `any` receiver, so adding `@types/p5` later will make these params fail at the `fill()` calls. That is the correct outcome and the signal to switch them to `p5.Color`.

## Mutation-tested, not just green

Green on a type-only change proves very little, so both halves were checked against a deliberate mutant, in the **final** shape of the code:

| Mutant | This PR | Old code restored |
|---|---|---|
| Loader resolves `mod.P5WrapperClassName` instead of `mod.ReactP5Wrapper` | **TS2345** | **0 errors** |
| `type P5Color = any` | **1 lint error** (`Unexpected any`) | n/a — rule was off |

Note that prop-level checking on this component is vacuous either way: `SketchProps` is `{[key: string]: unknown}`, so `P5WrapperProps` carries an index signature and accepts any prop name. The value here is in checking the **loader's** return type, not the props.

## Verification

- `pnpm typecheck` clean
- `pnpm lint` clean **with the rule enabled**
- `pnpm test` — 170 passed (17 files)
- `pnpm build` compiles
- **Runtime unchanged**: assertions, type arguments and parameter annotations all erase. `fishTankSketch.ts` emits byte-identical JavaScript.

`ssr: false` is load-bearing and untouched — p5 touches `window` at module scope, so a static import breaks the server render.
